extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in film analysis, creative writers, and scholars of slapstick/comedy and dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance for analyzing or creating slapstick film characters and narratives, especially how character, action, and mise-en-scène interact to produce comedy. Focuses on medium-specific techniques (film vs theatre) and how passive characters can be made psychologically rich.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-dimensionality of dramatic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be three-dimensional: physicality, sociology, and psychology (Egri's 'third dimension').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Egri emphasizes the role of psychology and the 'internal dialectics of character' as essential to creating a memorable play. When evaluating or writing, check that a character has not only external traits and social position but also interior drives and contradictions that can fuel conflict and progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action precedes character (Aristotle's view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Action reveals character: as Aristotle put it, action precedes character; observers derive motives from a character's motions and compile a picture of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat dramatic action as the primary vehicle for revealing interiority—in evaluation, ask whether what characters do allows audiences to infer motive and personality. Note the post that Aristotle discusses the 'appearance' of drama unfolding to crowds, so consider how performance and visible behavior communicate psychological information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passivity can be three-dimensional in film
rubrics_metrics.description: A passive comic persona (e.g., Harry Langdon's Odd Fellow) can nevertheless be psychologically insightful and three-dimensional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't assume passivity equals flatness. In film, especially silent-era slapstick, a character's passivity may be counterbalanced by the world's behavior and the film's formal devices; evaluate whether the surrounding mise-en-scène and narrative logic provide depth to a passive protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: External world/mise-en-scène should reflect interior states
rubrics_metrics.description: "Visuals in the outside should reflect the inside emotions" (Woody Allen; akin to Lacan's 'ex-timacy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authorial attention to background detail—setting, props, architectural quirks, repeated absences (e.g., lack of cops)—to externalize internal feelings. Assess whether the film's visual details and background elements meaningfully mirror or comment on the character's psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of background detail and props to externalize character
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects and background actions (an inanimate rag-doll double, long unexplained staircases, anonymous letters falling from the sky) can embody and communicate a character's inner life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or design props and background elements to function symbolically or comically so they reflect or complicate the protagonist's interiority rather than merely decorating the frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of absurd, dream-like, and structurally experimental logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative can be 'radically dream-like and structurally experimental'—odd jokes and illogical sequences can form the comedic logic rather than strict cause-and-effect realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or crafting slapstick, consider whether surreal or illogical elements cohere into a consistent tonal logic that supports comedy (rather than appearing as careless incoherence). Examples: anonymous letters falling, floors giving out, improbable entrances/exits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing unnecessary struggles as comedy rather than tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Unnecessary struggles—absurd obstacles imposed by the world—can evoke comedy instead of Sisyphean tragedy when staged and toned correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the film frames repetitive or pointless obstacles with comic timing, invention, and distance (so they read as humorous misfortune rather than bleak futility). Compare tone to Beckett, Flann O'Brien, or W.C. Fields to judge boundary between comic absurdity and tragic absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective subversion or deployment of genre conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing to employ or omit expected genre elements (for instance, Langdon 'rarely makes use of cops', which is 'extremely rare for the genre') affects narrative logic and character perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate decisions that subvert conventions: does the omission or inversion deepen theme, emphasize character traits, or destabilize audience expectations productively? Use such choices to probe the logic propelling story-lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-specific adaptation of dramatic principles (theatre vs film)
rubrics_metrics.description: Egri's theatre-centered rules (character, conflict, progression through dialectics) must be adapted for film, which can make internality visible through cinematic means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying dramatic-writing standards, account for the affordances of the medium: film allows background, camerawork, and editing to reflect psychology, so critiques or writing advice should translate theatrical prescriptions into cinematic techniques (mise-en-scène, visual motifs, editing rhythms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing abstraction in jokes with narrative placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes in the discussed film are 'half punch lines, half humdrum' and are 'abstractions — and featured in the background setting rather than in the decisions of our anti-hero.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluation/creation, check whether humorous elements function as background texture or as outcomes of character choice. Both strategies can work; ensure their placement supports the intended comedic effect and does not render the protagonist inert or the comedy aimless.
